description: Formal, textbook-style Learn content for the Mathalino Student App, mapped directly from the attached Rapid Mathematics Assessment (RMA) source materials. Each lesson follows a consistent 12-part instructional sequence (Objectives -> Introduction -> Explanation -> Key Concepts -> Worked Examples -> Guided Practice -> Independent Practice -> Real-Life Application -> Check Understanding -> Summary -> Challenge). This file supplies content only; it does not define or change the existing Learn screen UI (4 module cards: Number Sense, Operations, Fractions, Geometry).

moduleMappingNotes.data_and_probability: The RMA source materials do not define a separate 'Data & Probability' module in the Mathalino Learn section. This lesson was placed in Operations because the RMA item requires the learner to compute or compare quantities (tallies, totals, differences, or chance expressed as a fraction) rather than reason abstractly about numbers (Number Sense) or shapes/measurement (Geometry). This is a placement judgment, not a category defined in the RMA materials themselves.

modules.name: Number Sense
modules.description: Build confidence with numbers and place value.

topics.title: Counting, Reading, and Ordering Numbers to 100

objectives: Count up to 100, including counting up and down from a given number.
Read and write numerals up to 100.
Identify the number that is 1 more or 1 less than a given number.
Order numbers up to 20 from smallest to largest, and vice versa.
lessonSequence.introduction: Numbers are everywhere — on your house, on a calendar, on a bus. Today you will practice reading numbers, finding their neighbors, and putting them in order.
explanation: Step 1: Say numbers in order, starting from any number, going up (3, 4, 5...) or down (5, 4, 3...).
Step 2: To read a number, look at how it is written and say its name out loud (e.g., '9' is 'nine').
Step 3: Every number has a neighbor that is 1 more (count forward once) and 1 less (count backward once).
Step 4: To order numbers, find the smallest one first, then the next smallest, and so on.
keyConcepts: Counting up means saying numbers in increasing order; counting down means saying them in decreasing order.
'1 more' than a number = that number + 1. '1 less' than a number = that number − 1.
'Least to greatest' means arranging numbers from smallest to largest.

workedExamples.problem: What number is 1 more than 9?
workedExamples.solution: 9, then the next number is 10. So 1 more than 9 is 10.

workedExamples.problem: Arrange 3, 8, 9, 10, 12 from least to greatest.
workedExamples.solution: Find the smallest first (3), then 8, then 9, then 10, then 12: 3, 8, 9, 10, 12.

guidedPractice.problem: What number is 1 less than 9?
guidedPractice.hint: Count backward one step from 9.

guidedPractice.problem: Arrange 12, 3, 9 from least to greatest.
guidedPractice.hint: Which of the three is smallest? Which is biggest?

independentPractice: Write the number that is 1 more than 15.
Write the number that is 1 less than 20.
Arrange these numbers from greatest to least: 6, 2, 14, 9.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: When you line up at school by height or by number, you are ordering — just like ordering numbers from smallest to largest.
checkUnderstanding: What number is 1 more than 17?
Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: 4, 1, 8.
lessonSequence.summary: You can count forward and backward, read and write numbers up to 100, find a number's neighbors (1 more/1 less), and arrange numbers from smallest to largest.
challenge: Write the numbers from 90 to 100 in order.
What number is 1 more than the number that is 1 more than 8?

objectives: Determine the next term(s) in a repeating pattern of shapes, numbers, or rhythms.
lessonSequence.introduction: Have you noticed how a necklace of beads sometimes repeats the same shapes over and over? That repeating group is called a pattern.
explanation: Step 1: Look at the shapes or numbers shown, from left to right.
Step 2: Find the smallest group that repeats — this is called the 'pattern unit.'
Step 3: Once you know the pattern unit, you can predict what comes next by continuing the repeat.
keyConcepts: A pattern is a sequence that repeats the same group of items in the same order.
The 'pattern unit' is the smallest repeating group.

workedExamples.problem: Triangle, square, rectangle, triangle, square, rectangle, ___
workedExamples.solution: The pattern unit is: triangle, square, rectangle. After rectangle, it starts over, so the answer is triangle.

workedExamples.problem: Circle, half-circle, square, circle, half-circle, square, ___, ___
workedExamples.solution: The pattern unit is: circle, half-circle, square. The next two shapes are circle, half-circle.

guidedPractice.problem: Star, star, moon, star, star, moon, ___
guidedPractice.hint: What is the 3-item group that keeps repeating?
Which two numbers keep repeating?

independentPractice: Red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, ___
Draw the next two shapes: square, circle, circle, square, circle, circle, ___, ___
Clap, stomp, clap, stomp, clap, ___
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Patterns appear in the days of the week (they repeat every 7 days) and in songs (a chorus that repeats).
checkUnderstanding: What comes next: yellow, yellow, green, yellow, yellow, green, ___?
lessonSequence.summary: A pattern repeats the same group in the same order, so you can always predict what comes next.
challenge: Create your own 3-shape repeating pattern and show what the 10th shape would be.

modules.name: Operations
modules.description: Practice addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

objectives: Illustrate addition of numbers with sums up to 20 using objects or pictures.
Describe addition as 'counting up' and 'putting together.'
Add numbers with sums up to 100 without regrouping (2-digit + 1-digit, and 2-digit + 2-digit).
lessonSequence.introduction: If you have 3 candies and your friend gives you 4 more, how many do you have now? That's addition!
explanation: Step 1: Addition means combining two groups into one bigger group.
Step 2: Count all the objects in the first group, then all the objects in the second group.
Step 3: Put the groups together and count everything — this total is called the 'sum.'
Step 4: For written addition without regrouping, add the ones digits together, then the tens digits together.
keyConcepts: Addition combines two amounts into a total, called the sum.
The '+' sign means 'add' or 'put together.'
When adding 2-digit numbers, line up the ones and tens columns before adding.

workedExamples.problem: 3 popsicle sticks + 4 popsicle sticks = ?
workedExamples.solution: Put the 3 sticks and 4 sticks together and count all: 7 sticks.
Add the ones: 5 + 1 = 6. Add the tens: 1 + 2 = 3. The sum is 36.

guidedPractice.hint: Add the ones digits first: 1 + 3.

guidedPractice.problem: A bundle of 10 sticks and 5 loose sticks, plus a bundle of 10 and 2 loose sticks — how many in all?
guidedPractice.hint: Add the tens (bundles) together, then add the ones (loose sticks) together.

independentPractice: You have 8 marbles. Your friend gives you 9 more. How many marbles do you have now?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Counting your allowance after your parents give you more money is a real-life example of addition.
checkUnderstanding: What does the sum tell you when you add two groups together?
lessonSequence.summary: Addition puts two groups together to find the total, or sum. Add ones to ones and tens to tens.
challenge: 36 + 43 = ? (no regrouping needed — try it!)

objectives: Illustrate subtraction involving numbers up to 20 as 'taking away.'
Subtract numbers less than 100 without regrouping (2-digit − 1-digit, and 2-digit − 2-digit).
lessonSequence.introduction: If you have 5 cookies and you eat 3, how many are left? That's subtraction!
explanation: Step 1: Subtraction means taking some objects away from a group.
Step 2: Start with the total amount, then remove (cross out or cover) the amount being taken away.
Step 3: Count what is left — this is called the 'difference.'
Step 4: For written subtraction without regrouping, subtract the ones digits, then the tens digits.
keyConcepts: Subtraction takes an amount away from a total, leaving a difference.
The '−' sign means 'take away' or 'subtract.'
You cannot subtract more than what you started with.

workedExamples.problem: 5 counters, cover 3 of them. How many are left?
workedExamples.solution: 5 − 3 = 2. Two counters are left.
Subtract the ones: 5 − 0 = 5. Subtract the tens: 2 − 1 = 1. The difference is 15.

guidedPractice.hint: Subtract the ones digits: 2 − 2.

guidedPractice.problem: You have 15 stickers and give 4 to a friend. How many do you have left?
guidedPractice.hint: Start with 15, take away 4.

independentPractice: There are 20 birds on a wire. 6 fly away. How many birds are left?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Figuring out how much change you get back after paying for something uses subtraction.
lessonSequence.summary: Subtraction takes an amount away from a total, leaving a difference. Subtract ones from ones and tens from tens.
challenge: 48 − 26 = ? Show your work using tens and ones.

modules.name: Fractions
modules.description: Explore parts, wholes, and equivalent fractions.

topics.title: Halves and Fourths of a Whole

objectives: Illustrate one-half and one-fourth as parts of a whole.
Count halves and quarters.
lessonSequence.introduction: If you and your sibling share one sandwich equally, how much does each of you get? You each get one-half!
explanation: Step 1: A whole is one complete object or group (like one whole pizza).
Step 2: When a whole is split into 2 equal parts, each part is called one-half.
Step 3: When a whole is split into 4 equal parts, each part is called one-fourth (or one-quarter).
Step 4: The parts must be equal in size for the fraction name to be correct.
keyConcepts: One-half (1/2) means 1 out of 2 equal parts.
One-fourth (1/4) means 1 out of 4 equal parts.
The parts of a whole must be equal for fractions to make sense.

workedExamples.problem: A square is split into 2 equal parts, and 1 part is shaded. What fraction is shaded?
workedExamples.solution: 1 shaded part out of 2 equal parts = one-half.

workedExamples.problem: There are 8 breads and 4 plates. Each plate should get one-fourth of the breads. How many breads per plate?
workedExamples.solution: 8 breads ÷ 4 equal groups = 2 breads on each plate.

guidedPractice.problem: A candy bar is split into 4 equal pieces. You eat 1 piece. What fraction did you eat?
guidedPractice.hint: How many equal pieces make the whole bar?

guidedPractice.problem: 12 mangoes are shared equally between 2 baskets. How many mangoes are in each basket (one-half)?
guidedPractice.hint: Split 12 into 2 equal groups.

independentPractice: A pizza is cut into 2 equal slices. What fraction is 1 slice?
16 crayons are shared equally in 4 boxes. How many crayons are in each box?
Shade one-half of a rectangle divided into 2 equal parts.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Sharing a snack equally with a friend, or splitting a chore in half, uses the idea of halves.
checkUnderstanding: If a whole is split into 4 equal parts, what is the name for each part?
lessonSequence.summary: A whole split into 2 equal parts gives halves; split into 4 equal parts gives fourths. Parts must be equal.
challenge: If 20 candies are shared equally into 4 bags (one-fourth each), how many candies are in each bag?

modules.name: Geometry
modules.description: Learn shapes, space, measurement, and patterns.

objectives: Identify simple 2-dimensional shapes (triangle, rectangle, square) of different sizes and orientations.
lessonSequence.introduction: Shapes are all around us — a book is like a rectangle, a slice of pizza is like a triangle!
explanation: Step 1: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
Step 2: A rectangle has 4 sides, with opposite sides equal, and 4 square corners.
Step 3: A square has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners — it is a special rectangle.
Step 4: A shape keeps its name even if it is turned sideways or made bigger or smaller.
keyConcepts: Triangle = 3 sides, 3 corners.
Rectangle = 4 sides (opposite sides equal), 4 square corners.
Square = 4 equal sides, 4 square corners.
Turning or resizing a shape does not change its name.

workedExamples.problem: A set of rectangles of different sizes are shown. What are they called?
workedExamples.solution: They are all rectangles — size does not change the name.

workedExamples.problem: A square cutout is shown turned sideways (like a diamond). What is it still called?
workedExamples.solution: It is still a square, because it still has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners.

guidedPractice.problem: How many sides does a triangle have?
guidedPractice.hint: Think of a slice of pizza or a roof shape.

guidedPractice.problem: What is the difference between a square and a rectangle?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the length of all 4 sides.

independentPractice: Draw a triangle, a rectangle, and a square.
Sort these objects into triangle, rectangle, or square: a window, a road sign, a folder.
Is a shape with 4 equal sides always a square? Explain.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: A door is shaped like a rectangle, a folded sandwich can look like a triangle, and a tile can be a square.
checkUnderstanding: Name a shape with 3 sides.
Name a shape with 4 equal sides.
lessonSequence.summary: Triangles have 3 sides, rectangles have 4 sides with opposite sides equal, and squares have 4 equal sides.
challenge: Find 3 objects at home that are shaped like rectangles.

topics.title: Telling Time and Using a Calendar

objectives: Read and write time by the hour, half hour, and quarter hour using an analog clock.
Give the days of the week and months of the year in the correct order.
Determine the day and month of the year using a calendar.
lessonSequence.introduction: An analog clock has two hands that move to show the time — just like the hands on your favorite cartoon clock!
explanation: Step 1: The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes.
Step 2: When the long hand points to 12, it is exactly on the hour (e.g., 4:00).
Step 3: When the long hand points to 6, it is half past the hour (e.g., 4:30).
Step 4: The days of the week always repeat in the same order: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
keyConcepts: Short hand = hour. Long hand = minutes.
Long hand on 12 = o'clock. Long hand on 6 = half past.
There are 7 days in a week and 12 months in a year, always in the same order.

workedExamples.problem: The short hand is near 4, and the long hand is on 6. What time is it?
workedExamples.solution: The long hand on 6 means half past the hour, so it is 4:30.

workedExamples.problem: Today is Monday. What day is tomorrow? What day was yesterday?
workedExamples.solution: Tomorrow is Tuesday (the next day). Yesterday was Sunday (the day before).

guidedPractice.problem: The short hand is on 7 and the long hand is on 12. What time is it?
guidedPractice.hint: Long hand on 12 means exactly on the hour.

guidedPractice.problem: If today is Friday, what day comes next?
guidedPractice.hint: Think of the order of days of the week.

independentPractice: Draw clock hands to show 9:00.
Name the month that comes right after June.
If today is Wednesday, what was yesterday?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Reading a clock helps you know when to wake up, eat lunch, or watch your favorite show.
checkUnderstanding: What time does a clock show when the long hand points to 12 and the short hand points to 8?
lessonSequence.summary: An analog clock's short hand shows the hour and long hand shows the minutes. Days and months always follow the same order.
challenge: If today is the last day of a month, what is tomorrow's date likely to be?

objectives: Measure the length of an object or the distance between two objects using non-standard units.
Compare lengths and distances using non-standard units.
lessonSequence.introduction: Before rulers were common, people measured things using objects like sticks or their own hands!
explanation: Step 1: Choose a small object to use as your measuring unit (like a popsicle stick).
Step 2: Line up the units end-to-end along the object you are measuring, without gaps or overlaps.
Step 3: Count how many units fit — that is the length.
Step 4: To compare two lengths, count the units for each and see which has more units (longer) or fewer (shorter).
keyConcepts: A non-standard unit is any object used to measure, like a stick, a hand span, or a paperclip.
The unit must stay the same size each time you measure.
The object with more units is longer; fewer units means shorter.

workedExamples.problem: A ribbon lines up with 3 popsicle sticks. How long is the ribbon?
workedExamples.solution: The ribbon is 3 popsicle sticks long.

workedExamples.problem: Ribbon A is 3 sticks long. Ribbon B is 5 sticks long. Which is longer?
workedExamples.solution: 5 is greater than 3, so Ribbon B is longer.

guidedPractice.problem: A pencil lines up with 6 paperclips. How long is the pencil?
guidedPractice.hint: Count the paperclip units laid end to end.

guidedPractice.problem: A table is 10 hand-spans long, and a chair is 4 hand-spans long. Which is longer?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the two numbers of hand-spans.

independentPractice: Measure the length of a book using your hand span. How many hand spans long is it?
Compare two pencils by counting how many paperclips long each one is.
Which is longer: an object that is 8 sticks long, or one that is 5 sticks long?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Before you have a ruler nearby, you can estimate the length of a table using your own footsteps.
checkUnderstanding: If a rope is 7 sticks long and another rope is 4 sticks long, which rope is shorter?
lessonSequence.summary: Non-standard units (like sticks or hand spans) can measure and compare lengths, as long as the same unit is used each time.
challenge: Measure 3 objects around you using the same non-standard unit, and list them from shortest to longest.

modules.name: Number Sense
modules.description: Build confidence with numbers and place value.

objectives: Read and write numerals up to 1,000.
Represent numbers up to 1,000 using concrete/pictorial models and numerals.
Determine the place value and value of a digit in a 3-digit number.
lessonSequence.introduction: A 3-digit number has three 'homes' for its digits: hundreds, tens, and ones. Let's find out how to read them!
explanation: Step 1: In a 3-digit number, the digit farthest right is in the ones place.
Step 2: The middle digit is in the tens place.
Step 3: The digit farthest left is in the hundreds place.
Step 4: To find the value of a digit, multiply the digit by what its place is worth (ones = ×1, tens = ×10, hundreds = ×100).
keyConcepts: Place value tells you what a digit's position means (ones, tens, hundreds).
The value of a digit = digit × its place value (e.g., the 7 in 375 has a place value of tens, so its value is 7 × 10 = 70).
375 is read as 'three hundred seventy-five.'

workedExamples.problem: What is the place value of the digit 7 in 375?
workedExamples.solution: 375 has 3 in hundreds, 7 in tens, 5 in ones, so 7 is in the tens place.

workedExamples.problem: What is the value of the digit 7 in 375?
workedExamples.solution: 7 is in the tens place, so its value is 7 × 10 = 70.

guidedPractice.problem: Read the number 375 aloud.
guidedPractice.hint: Say the hundreds digit first, then 'and' the tens and ones.

guidedPractice.problem: What is the value of the digit 3 in 375?
guidedPractice.hint: Which place is the 3 in?

independentPractice: What is the place value of the 6 in 462?
What is the value of the digit 8 in 812?
Write the numeral for 'six hundred fifty-two.'
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Knowing place value helps you read prices, like knowing that ₱250 means 2 hundreds, 5 tens, and 0 ones.
checkUnderstanding: In the number 519, what is the value of the digit 1?
lessonSequence.summary: Every digit in a number has a place (ones, tens, hundreds) and a value based on that place.
challenge: Write the largest 3-digit number you can make using the digits 4, 9, and 2 (each used once).

objectives: Represent numbers up to 1,000 using models and numerals.
Order numbers up to 1,000 from smallest to largest, and vice versa.
lessonSequence.introduction: Which is bigger, 857 or 954? Comparing numbers is like comparing how tall two buildings are — check the biggest part first!
explanation: Step 1: To compare two numbers, first compare the digit in the highest place value (hundreds).
Step 2: If the hundreds digits are the same, compare the tens digits.
Step 3: If the tens digits are also the same, compare the ones digits.
Step 4: Use '>' for 'greater than' and '<' for 'less than.'
keyConcepts: Compare numbers starting from the leftmost (highest-value) digit.
'>' means greater than; '<' means less than.
A missing-digit problem can have more than one correct answer if several digits would work.

workedExamples.problem: Find the missing digit that makes __54 > 857 true.
workedExamples.solution: The hundreds digit of 857 is 8. To make the number greater, the missing digit must be 9, so 954 > 857.

workedExamples.problem: Compare 462 and 426. Which is greater?
workedExamples.solution: Hundreds are the same (4). Compare tens: 6 > 2, so 462 > 426.

guidedPractice.problem: Compare 305 and 350. Which is greater?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the tens digits since the hundreds are the same.

guidedPractice.problem: Find a missing digit: 2__0 > 240.
guidedPractice.hint: What tens digit would make this number bigger than 240?

independentPractice: Compare 189 and 198 using > or <.
Order these numbers from smallest to largest: 640, 460, 604.
Find a digit that makes 7_5 greater than 725.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Comparing numbers helps you know which item costs more when shopping, or which score is higher in a game.
checkUnderstanding: Which is greater: 512 or 521?
lessonSequence.summary: To compare numbers, look at the highest place value first, then move right if digits are equal.
challenge: List all the possible digits that could replace the blank in 3_6 to make it greater than 356.

objectives: Count by 2s, 5s, 10s, 20s, 50s, and 100s (not beyond 1,000).
Determine the next terms in increasing or decreasing patterns.
lessonSequence.introduction: Skip counting is like taking big jumps instead of little baby steps when counting!
explanation: Step 1: Find the difference between the given numbers in the pattern (how much it jumps each time).
Step 2: Check if the pattern is increasing (getting bigger) or decreasing (getting smaller).
Step 3: Apply the same jump to find the missing number.
keyConcepts: Skip counting means counting in equal jumps (by 2s, 5s, 10s, and so on) instead of by ones.
An increasing pattern adds the same amount each time; a decreasing pattern subtracts the same amount each time.

workedExamples.solution: Each number decreases by 10. After 40, the next number is 40 − 10 = 30.
Each number increases by 20. After 160, the next number is 160 + 20 = 180.

guidedPractice.hint: What number is each term jumping by?
Is this pattern increasing or decreasing? By how much?

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Skip counting by 5s helps you count coins quickly, like counting ₱5 coins.
checkUnderstanding: What is the next number in this pattern: 30, 40, 50, ___?
lessonSequence.summary: Skip counting jumps by the same amount each time. Find the jump size, then apply it to find missing numbers.
challenge: Create a skip-counting pattern that counts down by 50s from 500 to 0.

modules.name: Operations
modules.description: Practice addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

objectives: Add numbers with sums up to 1,000, with or without regrouping.
Solve word problems involving addition, including problems with money.
lessonSequence.introduction: Adding bigger numbers uses the same idea as adding small numbers — just with more digits to add!
explanation: Step 1: Line up the numbers by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds).
Step 2: Add the ones column first. If the sum is 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry (regroup) the ten to the tens column.
Step 3: Add the tens column (including any carried number), and regroup again if needed.
Step 4: Add the hundreds column last.
keyConcepts: Regrouping happens when a column's sum is 10 or more — you carry the extra ten to the next column.
Always add starting from the ones column.

workedExamples.solution: Ones: 2+4=6. Tens: 5+3=8. Hundreds: 1+2=3. Sum = 386.
Ones: 7+6=13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 5+3+1=9. Hundreds: 4. Sum = 493.

guidedPractice.hint: Add the ones first. Does it need regrouping?

guidedPractice.problem: Grade 2-Maya collected 128 bottles, Grade 2-Agila collected 63. How many bottles in all?
guidedPractice.hint: This is the same as the addition problem above — what operation do you need?

independentPractice: A vendor sold 215 mangoes in the morning and 128 in the afternoon. How many mangoes were sold in all?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Adding up your allowance savings across several days uses the same regrouping process.
lessonSequence.summary: Add numbers by place value, starting with ones, and regroup (carry) whenever a column's total is 10 or more.
challenge: 495 + 386 = ? (This one needs regrouping twice — try it!)

objectives: Illustrate subtraction as the inverse of addition.
Subtract numbers less than 1,000, with and without regrouping.
Solve 1- and 2-step subtraction word problems, including money.
lessonSequence.introduction: Subtraction can help you find your change after buying a snack — how much money is left?
explanation: Step 1: Line up the numbers by place value.
Step 2: Subtract the ones column first. If the top digit is smaller, regroup (borrow) a ten from the tens column.
Step 3: Subtract the tens column, borrowing from the hundreds if needed.
Step 4: Subtract the hundreds column last.
keyConcepts: Regrouping (borrowing) happens when the top digit in a column is smaller than the bottom digit.
Subtraction and addition are opposites — subtraction can 'undo' addition.

workedExamples.solution: Ones: 2−1=1. Tens: 9−2=7. Difference = 71.
Ones: 6−8 needs borrowing — borrow from tens: 16−8=8. Tens becomes 8 (after borrowing), 8−7=1. Hundreds: 3. Difference = 318.

guidedPractice.problem: A bag costs ₱225. Carla gives ₱250. How much change?
guidedPractice.hint: Subtract the cost from the amount given.
Check each column — do you need to borrow?

independentPractice: A vendor had 500 eggs and sold 236. How many eggs are left?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Finding out how much change you should receive after a purchase is real-world subtraction.
lessonSequence.summary: Subtract by place value from ones to hundreds, regrouping (borrowing) whenever the top digit is smaller.
challenge: 800 − 356 = ? (Notice the top number has zeros — think carefully about borrowing!)

objectives: Illustrate and write multiplication as repeated addition (equal groups, array, counting by multiples, equal jumps).
Multiply using the 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 multiplication tables.
Find a missing number in a multiplication or division sentence.
lessonSequence.introduction: If you have 4 bags with 3 apples in each bag, would you rather add 3+3+3+3, or use a faster way? That faster way is multiplication!
explanation: Step 1: Multiplication means adding the same number a certain number of times.
Step 2: The multiplication sentence 'a × b' means 'a groups of b' (or 'b groups of a').
Step 3: You can show multiplication with equal groups, an array (rows and columns), or jumps on a number line.
Step 4: To find a missing number, think about what times what gives the answer.
keyConcepts: Multiplication is repeated addition: 4 × 3 means 3+3+3+3, or 4 groups of 3.
'Product' is the answer to a multiplication problem.
Changing the order of the numbers being multiplied does not change the product (e.g., 3×4 = 4×3).

workedExamples.problem: 4 groups of 3 balls — how many balls in all?
workedExamples.solution: 4 groups of 3 = 4 × 3 = 12 balls.
3 groups of 4 = 4+4+4 = 12.

guidedPractice.problem: Which multiplication sentence describes 4 groups of 3 basketballs?
guidedPractice.hint: Match the number of groups and the number in each group to a × b.
What number times 10 gives 50?

independentPractice: Draw 3 groups of 4 stars and write the matching multiplication sentence.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: If you buy 5 packs of pencils with 2 pencils in each pack, multiplication (5 × 2) tells you the total quickly.
lessonSequence.summary: Multiplication is a fast way to add equal groups. a × b means a groups of b.
challenge: If 6 baskets have 5 mangoes each, how many mangoes are there in all?

objectives: Illustrate and write division expressions as equal sharing or repeated subtraction.
Divide using the 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 multiplication tables.
Solve division word problems, including problems involving money.
lessonSequence.introduction: If you have 12 candies to share equally with 3 friends, how many does each person get? That's division!
explanation: Step 1: Division means splitting a total into equal groups.
Step 2: 'Equal sharing' means giving out items one at a time until they run out evenly.
Step 3: 'Repeated subtraction' means subtracting the group size over and over until you reach zero, and counting how many times you subtracted.
Step 4: Division is the opposite of multiplication — if 3 × 4 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
keyConcepts: The 'quotient' is the answer to a division problem.
Division can mean 'how many in each group?' or 'how many equal groups can be made?'

workedExamples.problem: 12 balls shared equally into 3 groups — how many balls per group?
workedExamples.solution: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 balls in each group.

workedExamples.problem: 15 papayas, 3 per basket — how many baskets are needed?
workedExamples.solution: 15 ÷ 3 = 5 baskets.

guidedPractice.hint: How many groups of 5 fit into 25?
How many groups of 4 fit into 32?

independentPractice: 18 balls shared equally among 3 friends — how many balls does each friend get?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Sharing a box of 20 crayons equally among 4 classmates uses division to find out how many each person gets.
lessonSequence.summary: Division splits a total into equal groups. It is the opposite operation of multiplication.
challenge: 45 candies are shared equally among 5 children. How many candies does each child get?

modules.name: Fractions
modules.description: Explore parts, wholes, and equivalent fractions.

objectives: Read and write unit fractions in fraction notation.
Order unit fractions from smallest to greatest, and vice versa.
lessonSequence.introduction: Would you rather have 1 slice of a pizza cut into 2 pieces, or 1 slice of the same pizza cut into 8 pieces? The fewer cuts, the bigger the slice!
explanation: Step 1: A unit fraction always has 1 as the numerator (top number), like 1/2, 1/3, 1/4.
Step 2: The denominator (bottom number) tells you how many equal parts the whole is cut into.
Step 3: The more parts a whole is cut into, the smaller each part becomes.
Step 4: So, for unit fractions, a bigger denominator means a smaller fraction.
keyConcepts: A unit fraction has 1 as the numerator.
For unit fractions, the larger the denominator, the smaller the fraction (1/8 < 1/2).

workedExamples.problem: Which is bigger, 1/4 or 1/8?
workedExamples.solution: 1/4 has a smaller denominator, so it represents a bigger piece: 1/4 > 1/8.

workedExamples.problem: Arrange in order from smallest to greatest: 1/8, 1/6, 1/5, ?, 1/2
workedExamples.solution: Since the whole is being cut into fewer and fewer parts as we go, the missing fraction between 1/5 and 1/2 could be 1/4 or 1/3.

guidedPractice.problem: Which is smaller, 1/3 or 1/6?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the denominators — which whole is cut into more pieces?

guidedPractice.problem: Order 1/2, 1/10, 1/5 from smallest to largest.
guidedPractice.hint: Think about which denominator gives the smallest piece.

independentPractice: Which is bigger: 1/7 or 1/3?
Order these from largest to smallest: 1/4, 1/9, 1/2.
Write the unit fraction for 'one out of six equal parts.'
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Sharing a cake among more people (bigger denominator) means each person gets a smaller piece.
checkUnderstanding: Which is greater, 1/9 or 1/4?
lessonSequence.summary: A unit fraction has 1 as its numerator. The larger the denominator, the smaller the fraction.
challenge: Order these unit fractions from smallest to largest: 1/10, 1/2, 1/5, 1/3.

modules.name: Geometry
modules.description: Learn shapes, space, measurement, and patterns.

topics.title: Shapes, Patterns, and Surfaces
topics.rmaSource: Grade 2 Teacher's Booklet, Tasks I and J

objectives: Represent and describe circles, half circles, and quarter circles.
Determine the next terms in an increasing or decreasing shape pattern.
Identify the difference between straight and curved lines, and flat and curved surfaces of 3D objects.
lessonSequence.introduction: A whole pizza is a circle. Cut it once through the middle, and each piece is a half-circle. Cut it again, and you get quarter-circles!
explanation: Step 1: A circle is a round, whole shape. Cutting it in half gives two half-circles; cutting again gives quarter-circles.
Step 2: In a shape pattern, look for the repeating group just like with number patterns.
Step 3: A straight line goes directly from one point to another without bending; a curved line bends.
Step 4: A flat surface is smooth and even (like the side of a box); a curved surface bends around (like a ball).
keyConcepts: Circle → half-circle → quarter-circle shows how a whole shape splits into smaller equal parts.
A curved surface can roll (like a ball); a flat surface cannot.

workedExamples.problem: circle, half-circle, square, circle, half-circle, square, circle, ___, ___
workedExamples.solution: The pattern unit is circle, half-circle, square. After circle, the next two are half-circle, square.

workedExamples.problem: Which has a curved surface: a pyramid, a box, or a ball?
workedExamples.solution: A ball has a curved surface all around; the pyramid and box have flat surfaces.

guidedPractice.problem: Sort these into flat or curved surface: a can, a book, a globe.
guidedPractice.hint: Think about whether each object can roll.

guidedPractice.problem: triangle, triangle, circle, triangle, triangle, circle, ___
guidedPractice.hint: Find the repeating group of 3.

independentPractice: Draw a circle, then show how it looks cut into halves and then quarters.
List 2 objects with curved surfaces and 2 objects with flat surfaces.
Continue this pattern: square, square, triangle, square, square, triangle, ___, ___
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: A ball rolls because it has a curved surface, while a box stays in place because it has flat surfaces.
checkUnderstanding: Does a can (like a soda can) have a flat surface, a curved surface, or both?
lessonSequence.summary: Circles can be split into halves and quarters. Objects can have flat surfaces, curved surfaces, or both.
challenge: Find an object at home with both flat and curved surfaces, and describe which parts are which.

objectives: Measure and compare the length of objects, in meters or centimeters, and distance in meters, using appropriate tools.
lessonSequence.introduction: Now that you know how to measure with sticks, let's use a real ruler with centimeters!
explanation: Step 1: Line up one end of the object with the 0 mark on the ruler.
Step 2: Look at where the other end of the object lands on the ruler.
Step 3: Read the number at that point — that is the length in centimeters (cm).
Step 4: For longer distances, meters (m) are used instead of centimeters.
keyConcepts: Centimeters (cm) measure short lengths; meters (m) measure longer distances.
Always start measuring from the 0 mark on the ruler.

workedExamples.problem: A pencil lines up from 0 to 15 on a ruler. How long is the pencil?
workedExamples.solution: The pencil is 15 cm long.

workedExamples.problem: A crayon lines up from 0 to 8 on a ruler. How long is the crayon?
workedExamples.solution: The crayon is 8 cm long.

guidedPractice.problem: A ribbon lines up from 0 to 22 on a ruler. How long is the ribbon?
guidedPractice.hint: Read the number directly under the end of the ribbon.

guidedPractice.problem: Which is longer, an object that measures 12 cm or one that measures 9 cm?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the two centimeter values.

independentPractice: Measure a book using a ruler and write down its length in centimeters.
Compare 2 pencils by measuring each with a ruler and saying which is longer.
If your arm is about 40 cm long, is that closer to the length of a spoon or a broomstick?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Tailors use centimeters to measure fabric, and carpenters use them to measure wood for furniture.
checkUnderstanding: If a book measures from 0 to 25 on a ruler, how long is the book?
lessonSequence.summary: A ruler measures exact length in centimeters, starting from the 0 mark to the other end of the object.
challenge: Measure 3 objects at home in centimeters and arrange them from shortest to longest.

modules.name: Number Sense
modules.description: Build confidence with numbers and place value.

objectives: Represent numbers up to 10,000 using pictorial models (flats, longs, units, and thousands) and numerals.
lessonSequence.introduction: Numbers can get big! Base-ten blocks help you see what a big number is really made of.
explanation: Step 1: A 'unit' block equals 1. A 'long' block equals 10 units. A 'flat' block equals 10 longs (100 units).
Step 2: A 'thousands' block equals 10 flats (1,000 units).
Step 3: Count how many of each block type are shown, then add up their total values.
Step 4: Write the resulting number using its digits in the correct place-value positions.
keyConcepts: Unit = 1, Long = 10, Flat = 100, Thousands block = 1,000.
The total value of a picture is the sum of all the blocks' values.

workedExamples.problem: 5 flats + 1 long + 2 units represent what number?
4 thousands blocks + 6 flats + 2 units represent what number?

guidedPractice.problem: 3 flats + 4 longs + 5 units — what number is this?
guidedPractice.hint: Multiply each block by its value, then add.

guidedPractice.problem: 2 thousands + 3 flats + 1 unit — what number is this?
guidedPractice.hint: Remember thousands = 1,000 each.

independentPractice: 6 flats + 0 longs + 8 units — what number is this?
1 thousand + 9 flats + 9 longs + 9 units — what number is this?
Draw a base-ten block picture for the number 234.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Understanding place value with blocks helps you understand bigger numbers, like how many students are in a whole school district.
checkUnderstanding: What number is shown by 7 flats + 2 longs + 3 units?
lessonSequence.summary: Base-ten blocks (units, longs, flats, thousands) represent numbers by their place value, and their total tells you the number.
challenge: What is the largest number you can make using exactly 3 flats, 3 longs, and 3 units, if you can also add thousands blocks?

topics.title: Number Patterns with Larger Numbers
topics.rmaSource: Grade 3 Teacher's Booklet, Task C; RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 2

objectives: Determine the missing term(s) in a pattern with repeating and increasing, or repeating and decreasing, components.
lessonSequence.introduction: Patterns can now involve much bigger jumps — even jumps of 1,000!
explanation: Step 1: Compare two consecutive numbers in the pattern to find how much it changes.
Step 2: Check whether the pattern is increasing (going up) or decreasing (going down).
Step 3: Apply the same amount of change to find the next or missing number.
Step 4: For shape or bead patterns, find the repeating unit just as in earlier grades, but with more items in the unit.
keyConcepts: The 'common difference' is the fixed amount a number pattern increases or decreases by.
A repeating pattern with shapes can have more than 3 items in its repeating unit.

workedExamples.solution: Each number decreases by 1,000. After 6,000: 6,000 − 1,000 = 5,000.
Each number increases by 5. After 9,115: 9,115 + 5 = 9,120.

guidedPractice.hint: What is the common difference?

guidedPractice.problem: A repeating bead pattern of triangle, heart, circle — what are the next 3 beads after triangle, heart, circle, triangle, heart, circle?
guidedPractice.hint: Repeat the same 3-item unit.

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Understanding number patterns helps you predict things like savings growth if you save the same amount every week.
lessonSequence.summary: Find the common difference between numbers in a pattern, then apply it consistently to find missing terms.
challenge: Create a decreasing pattern that starts at 10,000 and decreases by 2,500 each time, for 4 terms.

modules.name: Operations
modules.description: Practice addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

topics.title: Adding Numbers up to 10,000
topics.rmaSource: Grade 3 Teacher's Booklet, Task D (part 2); RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 3

objectives: Find the sum of numbers up to 10,000, with and without regrouping.
lessonSequence.introduction: Adding 4-digit numbers uses the same steps as adding 3-digit numbers — just with a thousands column too!
explanation: Step 1: Line up the numbers by place value: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
Step 2: Add the ones column, regrouping if the sum is 10 or more.
Step 3: Add the tens, then hundreds, then thousands columns, regrouping as needed at each step.
Step 4: For word problems about the 'greatest sum,' think about which digit arrangement gives the largest possible number.
keyConcepts: Add starting from the ones column and move left, regrouping when a column totals 10 or more.
To make the greatest number from given digits, place the largest digit in the highest place value.

workedExamples.solution: Ones: 3+5=8. Tens: 7+2=9. Hundreds: 6+1=7. Thousands: 2. Sum = 2 798.
Ones: 5+4=9. Tens: 2+9=11, write 1 carry 1. Hundreds: 3+4+1=8. Thousands: 2+2=4. Sum = 4 819.

guidedPractice.problem: Arrange the digit cards 1, 3, 4, 6 to form the number that gives the greatest sum when added to 2,587.
guidedPractice.hint: To get the greatest sum, arrange the digits from largest to smallest.
Watch for regrouping in more than one column.

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Adding up the total number of students across several grade levels uses 4-digit addition.
lessonSequence.summary: Adding numbers up to 10,000 follows the same place-value steps as smaller addition, with a thousands column added.
challenge: 9 876 + 1 234 = ? Then explain which column(s) needed regrouping.

topics.title: Subtracting Numbers up to 10,000
topics.rmaSource: Grade 3 Teacher's Booklet, Task E; RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 10

objectives: Subtract numbers where both numbers are less than 10,000, with and without regrouping, including word problems.
lessonSequence.introduction: If you had ₱3,000 and bought groceries, how would you find your change? Subtraction with bigger numbers!
explanation: Step 1: Line up the numbers by place value.
Step 2: Subtract starting from the ones column, borrowing from the next column whenever the top digit is smaller.
Step 3: Continue subtracting through tens, hundreds, and thousands.
Step 4: For 'fill in the blank' problems using equal differences, check what happens to both sides of the equation equally.
keyConcepts: Borrowing (regrouping) moves 1 group from a higher place value into the column that needs more.
If you change both numbers in a subtraction problem by the same amount, the difference stays the same (e.g., 7 500 − 1 000 = 7 000 − 500).

workedExamples.solution: Ones: 8−0=8. Tens: 7−6=1. Hundreds: 4−2=2. Difference = 218.
Ones: 9−4=5. Tens: 0−2 needs borrowing... after regrouping, the difference is 1 085.

guidedPractice.problem: Maria bought groceries worth ₱2,456 and paid ₱3,000. How much change?
guidedPractice.hint: Subtract the cost from the amount paid.

guidedPractice.problem: Fill in the blank: 7 500 − 1 000 = 7 000 − ___
guidedPractice.hint: If both starting numbers decrease by 500, what happens to the second number?

independentPractice: A store had 4,500 items and sold 2,875. How many items are left?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Finding out how much money is left in a class fund after expenses uses this kind of subtraction.
lessonSequence.summary: Subtracting numbers up to 10,000 uses the same borrowing steps as smaller subtraction, extended to more place values.
challenge: 9 004 − 3 876 = ? (Notice the zeros — borrow carefully!)

topics.title: Multiplying 2- to 4-Digit Numbers
topics.rmaSource: Grade 3 Teacher's Booklet, Task F; RMA_4-6 Answer Key Items 1, 6, 11

objectives: Multiply 2- to 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number, with and without regrouping.
Multiply 2- to 4-digit numbers by a number whose only non-zero digit is the leading digit (e.g., ×20, ×300), with products up to 10,000.
Apply multiplication properties: order does not change the product, and any number multiplied by 1 equals itself.
lessonSequence.introduction: Multiplying bigger numbers is like multiplying small numbers, just with more digits to work through.
explanation: Step 1: To multiply a number by a 1-digit number, multiply each place value (ones, then tens, then hundreds) by that digit, regrouping when needed.
Step 2: To multiply by a number like 20, first multiply by 2, then multiply the result by 10 (add a zero).
Step 3: Remember: changing the order of numbers being multiplied does not change the answer (3×4 = 4×3).
Step 4: Any number multiplied by 1 stays the same.
keyConcepts: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 (like 20 or 300) means multiplying by the non-zero digit, then adding the zeros back.
Order does not matter in multiplication (the Commutative Property).
Any number × 1 = that same number (the Identity Property).

workedExamples.solution: 125 × 2 = 250. Then add a zero for the ×10: 250 × 10 = 2 500.

guidedPractice.hint: Multiply each digit by 4, starting from the ones, and regroup as needed.

guidedPractice.problem: If N is any number, what gives the same answer as 8 × N?
guidedPractice.hint: Which multiplication property applies here?

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: If a jeepney can carry 20 passengers and there are 15 trips in a day, multiplication finds the total passengers.
lessonSequence.summary: Multiply by place value, regroup as needed, and remember order and identity properties can make problems easier.
challenge: 1 25 × 300 = ? (Think about how many zeros to add.)

topics.title: Dividing 2- to 4-Digit Numbers
topics.rmaSource: Grade 3 Teacher's Booklet, Task G; RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 12

objectives: Divide 2- to 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number, with and without remainder.
Divide 2- to 4-digit numbers by 10, 100, and 1,000.
Find a missing number in a division sentence.
lessonSequence.introduction: Sometimes when you share things equally, there's a little bit left over — that's called a remainder!
explanation: Step 1: Ask how many times the divisor fits into the number being divided.
Step 2: If it doesn't divide evenly, the amount left over is the remainder.
Step 3: To divide by 10, 100, or 1,000, remove that many zeros from the end of the number.
Step 4: For missing-number problems, think about the related multiplication fact.
keyConcepts: A remainder is the amount left over when a number cannot be divided evenly.
Dividing by 10, 100, or 1,000 is the same as removing 1, 2, or 3 zeros.

workedExamples.solution: 6 fits into 18 exactly 3 times, no remainder: 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
9 × 4 = 36, which leaves 2 left over: 38 ÷ 9 = 4 remainder 2.

guidedPractice.problem: 168 mangoes shared equally in 8 baskets — how many mangoes per basket?
guidedPractice.hint: Think: how many groups of 8 fit into 168?
What number times 7 gives 56?

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Splitting a bag of 50 candies equally among 6 friends and figuring out the leftover uses division with remainder.
lessonSequence.summary: Division finds how many equal groups fit into a total, and any amount that doesn't fit evenly is the remainder.
challenge: 7 500 ÷ 1 000 = ? and 63 ÷ 8 = ? (with remainder)

topics.title: Collecting and Counting Data
topics.rmaSource: RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 4 (labeled Grade 3, Quarter 3)

objectives: Collect data from simple experiments with a small number of possible outcomes (e.g., tossing a coin or rolling a die).
lessonSequence.introduction: If you flip a coin 10 times, will you always get exactly 5 heads and 5 tails? Let's find out by counting!
explanation: Step 1: Record the result of each trial (like each coin toss) in order.
Step 2: Use tally marks or a table to count how many times each outcome happened.
Step 3: Add up the tallies for the outcome you are asked about.
keyConcepts: A trial is one single try, like one coin toss.
Recording results in a table makes counting outcomes easier and more accurate.

workedExamples.problem: A coin is tossed 10 times: Head, Head, Tail, Tail, Head, Tail, Tail, Head, Head, Head. How many heads?
workedExamples.solution: Counting all the 'Head' results: 1st, 2nd, 5th, 8th, 9th, 10th = 6 heads.

guidedPractice.problem: If the same 10 tosses had 6 heads, how many tails were there?
guidedPractice.hint: 10 total tosses minus the number of heads.

independentPractice: A die is rolled 6 times and lands on: 3, 5, 3, 2, 3, 6. How many times did it land on 3?
Flip a real or imaginary coin 10 times and tally your results.
Out of 20 tosses, 12 were heads. How many were tails?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Weather reporters collect daily rain/no-rain data over a month to see patterns, just like tallying coin tosses.
checkUnderstanding: If a coin is tossed 8 times and lands on heads 5 times, how many times did it land on tails?
lessonSequence.summary: Collecting data means recording and tallying results from repeated trials to count outcomes accurately.
challenge: Design your own 10-trial experiment (like flipping a coin) and predict how many of each outcome you expect before you try it.

topics.moduleMappingNote: The RMA source materials do not define a separate 'Data & Probability' module in the Mathalino Learn section. This lesson was placed in Operations because the RMA item requires the learner to compute or compare quantities (tallies, totals, differences, or chance expressed as a fraction) rather than reason abstractly about numbers (Number Sense) or shapes/measurement (Geometry). This is a placement judgment, not a category defined in the RMA materials themselves.

modules.name: Fractions
modules.description: Explore parts, wholes, and equivalent fractions.

topics.title: Adding and Subtracting Similar Fractions
topics.rmaSource: Grade 3 Teacher's Booklet, Task A; RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 7

objectives: Add and subtract similar fractions (same denominator) using models.
lessonSequence.introduction: If a pizza is cut into 8 equal slices, and you eat 3 slices, how much of the pizza is left?
explanation: Step 1: Similar fractions have the same denominator (bottom number).
Step 2: To add similar fractions, add only the numerators (top numbers) and keep the denominator the same.
Step 3: To subtract similar fractions, subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator the same.
Step 4: Check if your answer can be simplified.
keyConcepts: Similar fractions share the same denominator.
Add or subtract only the numerators when denominators match; the denominator stays the same.

workedExamples.problem: 1/8 shaded + 2/8 shaded = ?
workedExamples.solution: Add the numerators: 1+2=3. Keep the denominator: 3/8.

workedExamples.problem: A loaf of bread minus 3/8 given away — how much is left?
workedExamples.solution: 1 whole = 8/8. 8/8 − 3/8 = 5/8 of the bread is left.

guidedPractice.hint: Add only the numerators.
Subtract only the numerators.

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Sharing a chocolate bar cut into equal pieces and tracking how many pieces are eaten uses similar fractions.
lessonSequence.summary: For similar fractions, add or subtract the numerators only, and keep the denominator the same.
challenge: 6/8 − 5/8 = ? Can this answer be simplified further?

topics.title: Fractions Equal to and Greater Than One

objectives: Represent fractions that are equal to one and greater than one using models.
lessonSequence.introduction: Can a fraction be bigger than a whole pizza? Yes — if you have more than one whole pizza cut into equal slices!
explanation: Step 1: A fraction is equal to 1 whole when the numerator and denominator are the same (e.g., 2/2, 5/5).
Step 2: A fraction is greater than 1 whole when the numerator is bigger than the denominator (e.g., 3/2).
Step 3: To shade a fraction greater than 1, you need more than one whole region, each divided into equal parts.
keyConcepts: Numerator = denominator means the fraction equals 1 whole.
Numerator > denominator means the fraction is greater than 1 whole.

workedExamples.problem: Shade 3/2 of a region using 5 whole regions each split into halves.
workedExamples.solution: 3/2 means 3 half-pieces. Shade 1 whole region (2 halves) plus 1 more half from another region.

guidedPractice.problem: Is 4/4 equal to, less than, or greater than 1 whole?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the numerator and denominator.

guidedPractice.problem: Is 5/3 equal to, less than, or greater than 1 whole?
guidedPractice.hint: Compare the numerator and denominator.

independentPractice: Shade 5/4 using whole regions split into fourths.
Is 7/7 equal to 1 whole? Explain.
Is 9/5 greater than 1 whole? Explain.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: If you need 1 and a half pizzas for a party, you are using a fraction greater than 1 (3/2 pizzas).
checkUnderstanding: Is 6/5 equal to, less than, or greater than 1 whole?
lessonSequence.summary: A fraction equals 1 whole when numerator = denominator, and is greater than 1 whole when numerator > denominator.
challenge: Show 7/3 using whole regions split into thirds. How many whole regions do you need at least?

modules.name: Geometry
modules.description: Learn shapes, space, measurement, and patterns.

objectives: Measure mass in grams, kilograms, and/or milligrams using appropriate measuring tools.
lessonSequence.introduction: A balance scale tips to the heavier side — just like a seesaw!
explanation: Step 1: A balance scale is level when both sides have the same mass.
Step 2: If known weights (like cubes) balance an object, the object's mass equals the total mass of the weights.
Step 3: To find total mass, multiply the number of equal weights by the mass of each weight.
keyConcepts: Mass is measured in grams (g), kilograms (kg), or milligrams (mg).
A balanced scale means both sides have equal mass.

workedExamples.problem: A bag balances against 5 cubes, each with a mass of 10 grams. What is the mass of the bag?
workedExamples.solution: 5 × 10 g = 50 g. The bag has a mass of 50 grams.

guidedPractice.problem: A toy balances against 8 cubes, each 5 grams. What is the toy's mass?
guidedPractice.hint: Multiply the number of cubes by the mass of each cube.

independentPractice: A book balances against 12 cubes, each 20 grams. What is the book's mass?
If a fruit has a mass of 150 grams, and each weight cube is 25 grams, how many cubes balance it?
Order these masses from lightest to heaviest: 250 g, 1 kg, 500 g.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Bakers use grams to measure ingredients like flour and sugar precisely for recipes.
checkUnderstanding: A box balances against 6 cubes, each 15 grams. What is the box's mass?
lessonSequence.summary: A balance scale shows equal mass on both sides; multiply the number of weights by their individual mass to find total mass.
challenge: If 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams, how many grams is 3.5 kilograms?

objectives: Recognize and draw parallel, intersecting, and perpendicular lines.
Identify and draw line segments of equal length using a ruler.
lessonSequence.introduction: Look at a ladder — the two long side rails never touch. Now look at a plus sign (+) — the two lines cross in the middle!
explanation: Step 1: Parallel lines are always the same distance apart and never meet, no matter how far they extend.
Step 2: Intersecting lines cross each other at one point.
Step 3: Perpendicular lines are a special type of intersecting lines that cross to form a square (90°) corner.
Step 4: To check if line segments are equal, measure each one with a ruler and compare.
keyConcepts: Parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart.
Intersecting lines cross at one point.
Perpendicular lines intersect to form a right angle (square corner).

workedExamples.problem: Which edges of a rectangular box are parallel?
workedExamples.solution: The top and bottom edges of the same face are parallel — they never meet.

workedExamples.problem: Which edges of a rectangular box are perpendicular?
workedExamples.solution: Two edges that meet at a corner and form a square angle, like the side edge and the bottom edge.

guidedPractice.problem: Trace two edges of a box that intersect.
guidedPractice.hint: Look for two edges that share a corner point.

guidedPractice.problem: Trace two line segments in a box that appear to be the same length.
guidedPractice.hint: Use a ruler to measure and compare.

independentPractice: Draw two parallel lines.
Draw two perpendicular lines.
Name 2 objects around you that show parallel lines (like railroad tracks).
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Railroad tracks are parallel lines, and the corner of a picture frame shows perpendicular lines.
checkUnderstanding: What do we call two lines that cross to form a square corner?
lessonSequence.summary: Parallel lines never meet, intersecting lines cross at a point, and perpendicular lines cross to form a right angle.
challenge: Find 3 examples of perpendicular lines in your classroom or home.

topics.title: Comparing Areas of Squares and Rectangles

objectives: Solve problems involving the areas of squares and rectangles.
lessonSequence.introduction: If you cut a rectangle and rearrange the pieces into a square, does the amount of space it covers change?
explanation: Step 1: Area is the amount of flat space a shape covers.
Step 2: When you cut a shape and rearrange the same pieces (without removing or adding anything), the total area stays the same.
Step 3: Compare the resulting shape's area to the original by thinking about whether any material was added or lost.
keyConcepts: Cutting and rearranging the same material does not change the total area.
Area problems can be solved by reasoning about the pieces, not just by calculating with numbers.

workedExamples.problem: A rectangular cutout is cut into two equal parts to form a square cutout. How does the square's area compare to the rectangle's?
workedExamples.solution: Since no material was added or removed — only rearranged — the square's area is the same as the original rectangle's area.

guidedPractice.problem: If you cut a square piece of paper in half and rearrange the two halves, does the total area of the new shape change?
guidedPractice.hint: Think about whether the paper's amount changed.

independentPractice: A rectangle is cut into 4 equal strips and rearranged into a new shape. Compare the areas.
Explain, in your own words, why cutting and rearranging doesn't change total area.
If a rectangle has an area of 24 square units and is rearranged into a different shape, what is the new shape's area?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Tailors rearrange fabric pieces to cut clothing patterns without wasting fabric, relying on this same idea about area.
checkUnderstanding: If a shape is cut and rearranged without adding or removing pieces, does its area increase, decrease, or stay the same?
lessonSequence.summary: Cutting a shape into pieces and rearranging them does not change the total area, as long as nothing is added or removed.
challenge: Draw a rectangle, cut it (on paper) into 2 triangles, and explain why both triangles together still equal the rectangle's original area.

topics.title: Sliding Shapes (Translation)
topics.rmaSource: RMA_4-6 Answer Key Item 5 (labeled Grade 3, Quarter 4)

objectives: Describe and draw the effect of a two-direction, multi-step slide (translation) on a basic shape.
lessonSequence.introduction: Imagine sliding a book across a table — it moves without turning or flipping. That's called a translation!
explanation: Step 1: A slide (translation) moves a shape in a straight direction without rotating or flipping it.
Step 2: A slide can happen in more than one direction, like 'right' and 'down' together.
Step 3: Count the grid squares for each direction and move every point of the shape the same amount.
Step 4: The shape's size and orientation stay exactly the same after sliding — only its position changes.
keyConcepts: A translation (slide) moves a shape without turning or flipping it.
Every point of the shape moves the same distance and direction.

workedExamples.problem: Slide a triangle 2 units to the right and 3 units down. Where does it land?
workedExamples.solution: Move every corner of the triangle 2 squares right, then 3 squares down, keeping the same size and shape.

guidedPractice.problem: Slide a square 3 units to the right and 1 unit down on a grid.
guidedPractice.hint: Move each corner point the same amount.

independentPractice: Slide a rectangle 4 units left and 2 units up. Describe its new position.
If a shape's corner started at grid position (2,3) and slides 3 right and 1 down, where is the new corner?
Draw a shape on grid paper, then slide it 2 right and 2 down.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Moving a game piece across a board game grid is an example of a translation (slide).
checkUnderstanding: What happens to the size and shape of a figure after it is translated (slid)?
lessonSequence.summary: A translation slides a shape in one or more directions without changing its size, shape, or orientation.
challenge: If a shape is slid 5 right and 5 down, then slid again 2 left and 3 up, where does it end up compared to its starting position?

modules.name: Number Sense
modules.description: Build confidence with numbers and place value.
modules.note: No RMA item in the attached Grade 4-6 answer key was explicitly labeled as a Grade 4 'Number Sense' (place value / number representation) competency. The Grade 4 items that involve numbers (addition and subtraction of large numbers) are computation skills and are listed under Operations instead. This gap is documented here rather than inventing a Grade 4 Number Sense lesson.

modules.name: Operations
modules.description: Practice addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

topics.title: Adding and Subtracting Numbers up to 1,000,000

objectives: Add and subtract numbers where both numbers are less than 1,000,000, with and without regrouping.
lessonSequence.introduction: From thousands, we now work with numbers up to a million — like counting a whole city's population!
explanation: Step 1: Line up very large numbers carefully by place value, from ones up through hundred-thousands.
Step 2: Add or subtract column by column, starting from the ones place.
Step 3: Regroup (carry for addition, borrow for subtraction) whenever needed, watching zeros carefully.
Step 4: Check your answer by estimating — does it seem like a reasonable size?
keyConcepts: The same regrouping rules from smaller numbers apply to 6-digit numbers — there are just more columns.
Zeros in the number being subtracted from require extra careful borrowing across several columns.

workedExamples.solution: Borrowing across the zeros: 900,000 − 87,246 = 812,754.
Adding by place value with regrouping: 452,042 + 38,594 = 490,636.

guidedPractice.hint: Watch the zeros carefully when borrowing.
Line up the digits by place value before adding.

lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Government agencies add and subtract large population or budget figures using this same process.
lessonSequence.summary: Adding and subtracting numbers up to 1,000,000 uses the same place-value process as smaller numbers, with careful attention to zeros.
challenge: 500 005 − 249 876 = ? Explain each regrouping step.

topics.title: Dividing 3- to 4-Digit Numbers by a 1-Digit Number

objectives: Divide 3- to 4-digit numbers by 1-digit numbers, with and without regrouping.
lessonSequence.introduction: If a school collects money and needs to split it fairly among all grade levels, division makes it fair for everyone!
explanation: Step 1: Start dividing from the leftmost digit of the number being divided.
Step 2: Find how many times the divisor fits into that part of the number.
Step 3: Write the result, subtract, bring down the next digit, and repeat.
Step 4: Continue until every digit has been brought down and divided.
keyConcepts: Long division works digit by digit, from left to right.
If there's a remainder at the very end, the division did not come out evenly.

workedExamples.problem: ₱8,700 divided equally among 6 grade levels — how much per grade level?
workedExamples.solution: 8,700 ÷ 6 = 1,450. Each grade level receives ₱1,450.

guidedPractice.hint: Divide starting from the leftmost digit and work through each place.

independentPractice: A school raised ₱9,600 and wants to divide it equally among 8 classrooms. How much does each classroom get?
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Splitting a fundraising total equally among several school clubs uses this kind of division.
lessonSequence.summary: Divide 3- to 4-digit numbers by working through each place value from left to right, one digit at a time.
challenge: 7 236 ÷ 6 = ? Show each step of your long division.

topics.title: Reading and Comparing Data in Graphs

objectives: Interpret data presented in tabular form or in a single line graph.
lessonSequence.introduction: A line graph is like a picture story of numbers changing over time — did something go up, down, or stay the same?
explanation: Step 1: Look at what the two axes of the graph represent (for example, months and number of books).
Step 2: Find the value for each point on the graph.
Step 3: To find the largest decrease, compare each pair of consecutive points and find which pair has the biggest drop.
Step 4: A steeper downward line means a bigger decrease; a steeper upward line means a bigger increase.
keyConcepts: A line graph shows how a value changes across categories (often time periods).
The steepest drop between two points shows the largest decrease.

workedExamples.problem: A line graph of books read shows: August 30, September 20, October 25, November 19, December 15. Which months had the largest decrease?
workedExamples.solution: Compare each drop: Aug→Sep (−10), Sep→Oct (+5), Oct→Nov (−6), Nov→Dec (−4). The largest decrease is August to September.

guidedPractice.problem: If a graph shows sales of 50, 45, 60, 30 over four weeks, between which two weeks was the largest decrease?
guidedPractice.hint: Calculate the difference between each pair of consecutive weeks.

independentPractice: A graph shows temperatures of 30°C, 32°C, 28°C, 31°C over 4 days. Between which two days was the largest decrease?
Explain what it means when a line graph goes downward.
Create a simple line graph of your own weekly savings for 4 weeks and find the largest increase.
lessonSequence.realLifeApplication: Doctors use line graphs to track a patient's temperature or weight over time and spot sudden changes.
checkUnderstanding: If a value goes from 40 to 25, how much did it decrease?
lessonSequence.summary: A line graph shows how values change over time; comparing consecutive points reveals the largest increase or decrease.
challenge: Given the points 10, 40, 15, 45, 20 across 5 periods, which two consecutive periods show the greatest increase?
